summary.text: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, hiding the Sun from a small part of Earth, totally or partially.
The alignment occurs about every six months, during eclipse season, at new moon, when the Moon's orbital plane is closest to the plane of Earth's orbit.
In a total eclipse the Sun's disk is fully obscured, while in partial and annular eclipses only part of the Sun is obscured.

facts.label: Total eclipses worldwide
facts.value: Somewhere on Earth every 18 months on average

facts.label: Eclipses per year
facts.value: At least two, up to five

items.prompt: Every month the Moon sits between Earth and the Sun at new moon, yet most months nothing is blocked. Why?

options.label: Its orbit is tilted, so its shadow usually misses Earth
It is too small to ever cover the Sun
Earth's shadow hides it from the Sun
The Sun's glare outshines it each month

items.explain: Because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit, its shadow usually misses Earth, so eclipses happen only in eclipse seasons.

items.prompt: You watch a total eclipse from start to finish. When is it safe to look with no eye protection?

options.label: Whenever any part of the Sun is hidden
Only while the Sun's disk is fully hidden
Any time the sky is a little dimmer
Never; protection is needed throughout

items.explain: Looking directly at the Sun can cause permanent eye damage, but the total phase is safe to view without protection.

items.prompt: The Moon is farther than usual from Earth at the moment it lines up with the Sun, so it looks smaller. What happens?

options.label: It still fully covers the Sun, with a thinner shadow
No eclipse can happen at all
It cannot fully cover the Sun, so the eclipse is annular
A lunar eclipse happens instead

items.explain: Differences in the Moon's distance change its apparent size, which leads to the difference between total and annular eclipses. A total eclipse needs the Moon closer than average.

items.prompt: Millions of people can watch a lunar eclipse from home. Who can see a particular solar eclipse?

options.label: Everyone on the day side of Earth, equally
Everyone on the night side of Earth
Only people living at the equator
People in a relatively small area of the world

items.explain: A solar eclipse can only be viewed from a relatively small area of the world, unlike a lunar eclipse.

items.prompt: You stand in the larger, lighter part of the Moon's shadow rather than the small dark core. What do you see?

options.label: A partial eclipse
A total eclipse
An annular eclipse
No eclipse at all

items.explain: The penumbra is the larger light gray area where a partial eclipse can be seen; the umbra gives a total eclipse and the antumbra an annular one.

items.prompt: Can astronomers say when an eclipse will happen hundreds of years from now?

options.label: No; eclipses are random events
Only a few years ahead, as the Moon's orbit shifts too fast
Yes, with high accuracy
Only for total eclipses

items.explain: Eclipses hundreds of years into the future may now be predicted with high accuracy.
